items.stem: Philippe Bourgois's urban migrant community was in:
items.answer: East Harlem (El Barrio), New York
items.markingKey: East Harlem (El Barrio), New York. In Search of Respect (1995).

items.stem: Explain the difference between humanitarian control and humanitarian care.
items.answer: Humanitarian care provides food, shelter and health; humanitarian control registers, counts and restricts movement. Agier argues the two are combined.
items.markingKey: Humanitarian care provides food, shelter and health; humanitarian control registers, counts and restricts movement. Agier argues the two are combined. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why refugee camps can become semi-permanent places.
items.answer: Conflicts last for years and return or resettlement is blocked, so camps develop markets, schools, politics and new identities while remaining legally "temporary".
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Conflicts last for years and return or resettlement is blocked, so camps develop markets, schools, politics and new identities while remaining legally "temporary". (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using Bourgois's In Search of Respect (among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)) as your example, describe how identity is shown.
items.answer: Dealers built a "street culture" of resistance in which they sought the respect and dignity denied to them in mainstream work, yet that culture also drew them into self-destruction and violence.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Dealers built a "street culture" of resistance in which they sought the respect and dignity denied to them in mainstream work, yet that culture also drew them into self-destruction and violence. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995), among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to identity. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Using Malkki's Mishamo camp as an example, explain camp space and identity.
items.answer: Mishamo was an agricultural settlement where Hutu refugees from Burundi farmed under Tanzanian administration and built a collective history of exile. The camp's isolation and administration helped produce a strong national identity of purity and exile.
items.markingKey: Context (Mishamo was an agricultural settlement where Hutu refugees from Burundi farmed under Tanzanian administration and built a collective history of exile.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the camp's isolation and administration helped produce a strong national identity of purity and exile. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to camp space and identity.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the camp market, Abdi runs a shop made of corrugated iron that sells phone cards, pasta and solar lamps. He arrived as a boy in 1992 and his children were born here. The agency calls the shop an "income-generating activity"; Abdi calls it "my business". He cannot legally leave the camp to buy stock, so a Kenyan trader brings goods in his lorry. When the agency announced the camp would close, Abdi laughed. "They have closed it five times. Each time, I paint the shop again."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a refugee camp in Kenya.

Using the key concept of space, place and time, explain how the text shows a refugee camp becoming a lasting place. Support each step of your explanation with evidence from the extract.
items.answer: Decades of residence, children born in the camp, a market and trade networks with Kenyan traders show the camp as a "camp-city" (Agier); restrictions on leaving show humanitarian control; contrasting labels ("income-generating activity" vs "my business") show different classifications of refugee agency; repeated closure announcements and repainting show the permanence of the "temporary".
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Decades of residence, children born in the camp, a market and trade networks with Kenyan traders show the camp as a "camp-city" (Agier); restrictions on leaving show humanitarian control; contrasting labels ("income-generating activity" vs "my business") show different classifications of refugee agency; repeated closure announcements and repainting show the permanence of the "temporary". Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Define the term "humanitarian government".
items.answer: Michel Agier's term for the management of displaced populations by agencies combining care with control
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: Michel Agier's term for the management of displaced populations by agencies combining care with control. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "Refugee camps are short-term shelters that close quickly." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many camps last decades (Dadaab since 1991, Palestinian camps since 1948), becoming camp-cities.
items.markingKey: Many camps last decades (Dadaab since 1991, Palestinian camps since 1948), becoming camp-cities. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The process, often encouraged by states, of nomadic people settling permanently in one place"?
options: transhumance
sedentarism
sedentarisation
il-rah
items.answer: sedentarisation
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of sedentarisation.

items.stem: Explain why mobility is an adaptation rather than a sign of backwardness.
items.answer: Moving herds follows seasonal pasture and water, uses marginal environments efficiently and spreads risk, so mobility is a rational strategy for dry or cold environments.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Moving herds follows seasonal pasture and water, uses marginal environments efficiently and spreads risk, so mobility is a rational strategy for dry or cold environments. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Freya writes: "Nomads wander aimlessly without territory." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Nomads move along known routes with recognised rights and schedules (Barth's il-rah) and have detailed knowledge of territory.
items.markingKey: Nomads move along known routes with recognised rights and schedules (Barth's il-rah) and have detailed knowledge of territory. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In late spring the Kyzyl family loads the yurt onto a Kamaz truck and drives the sheep up to the summer pastures, a journey that took two weeks on horseback in Grandfather Bolat's time and now takes two days. Bolat still rides behind the flock. His grandson films the move on his phone and posts it with the caption "nomad life". The pasture they use was assigned to a collective farm in Soviet times; now it is leased from the district office, and this year a mining company has fenced part of it.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a herding family in Kazakhstan.

Explain how the text shows change and continuity in pastoral movement, using one or more anthropological concepts. Link the actions described to wider social, economic or political conditions.
items.answer: Seasonal transhumance continues (summer pastures, flock movement, grandfather on horseback), but technology (truck, phone), Soviet collectivisation and post-Soviet leasing, and mining fences change how movement is organised and who controls land; the grandson's post shows identity as "nomad" being performed and valued even as practices change.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Seasonal transhumance continues (summer pastures, flock movement, grandfather on horseback), but technology (truck, phone), Soviet collectivisation and post-Soviet leasing, and mining fences change how movement is organised and who controls land; the grandson's post shows identity as "nomad" being performed and valued even as practices change. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that nomadic pastoralism has no future in the modern world. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: Pastoralism is under pressure but is adapting; its future depends on land rights and state policy.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: land loss, borders and climate change threaten herding; young people move to towns; states promote settlement; pastoralists adapt using trucks, phones and markets (Chatty); pastoralism is efficient in drylands; Indigenous rights movements defend mobility. Suitable ethnographies include Barth's Nomads of South Persia, Evans-Pritchard's The Nuer, Vitebsky's The Reindeer People. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Pastoralism is under pressure but is adapting; its future depends on land rights and state policy. items.stem: Define the term "pastoralism".
items.answer: A way of life based on herding domesticated animals such as cattle, camels, sheep, goats or reindeer
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a way of life based on herding domesticated animals such as cattle, camels, sheep, goats or reindeer. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between mobility as adaptation and sedentarisation as development.
items.answer: Seeing mobility as adaptation values pastoralists' knowledge of environments; seeing sedentarisation as development assumes settled life is progress – a view many anthropologists criticise.
items.markingKey: Seeing mobility as adaptation values pastoralists' knowledge of environments; seeing sedentarisation as development assumes settled life is progress – a view many anthropologists criticise. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to Fredrik Barth, Nomads of South Persia: The Basseri Tribe of the Khamseh Confederacy (1961), explain how the key concept of power helps us to understand nomadism and pastoralist movement.
items.answer: The chief (khan) coordinated the migration and mediated between the tribe, the state and settled villagers.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The chief (khan) coordinated the migration and mediated between the tribe, the state and settled villagers. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Fredrik Barth, Nomads of South Persia: The Basseri Tribe of the Khamseh Confederacy (1961), among Basseri pastoralists of Fars province, Iran (fieldwork 1958)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Briefly describe Hodgson's Maasai in northern Tanzania and explain what it reveals about change in pastoral societies.
items.answer: Development projects registered cattle to men and promoted ranching schemes, while land was lost to farms and conservation areas. State and development interventions transformed pastoral livelihoods and reduced women's rights over livestock.
items.markingKey: Context (Development projects registered cattle to men and promoted ranching schemes, while land was lost to farms and conservation areas.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: state and development interventions transformed pastoral livelihoods and reduced women's rights over livestock. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to change in pastoral societies.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "structure and agency in mobility".
items.answer: The balance between forces that compel or block movement and people's capacity to choose how and where to move
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the balance between forces that compel or block movement and people's capacity to choose how and where to move. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why identity among mobile people is often situational.
items.answer: Mobile people interact with different audiences – officials, employers, kin, other migrants – and present different identities depending on the risks and opportunities of each setting.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Mobile people interact with different audiences – officials, employers, kin, other migrants – and present different identities depending on the risks and opportunities of each setting. items.stem: Explain the difference between nomadic movement and migrant movement.
items.answer: Nomadic movement is cyclical and part of a pastoral way of life; migrant movement is usually a longer-term relocation for work, safety or family, though both can be circular.
items.markingKey: Nomadic movement is cyclical and part of a pastoral way of life; migrant movement is usually a longer-term relocation for work, safety or family, though both can be circular. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Levitt's The Transnational Villagers (among migrants from Miraflores, Dominican Republic, and their community in Jamaica Plain, Boston) as your example, describe how belonging is shown.
items.answer: Migrants belonged to two places at once, joining village development and politics from Boston.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Migrants belonged to two places at once, joining village development and politics from Boston. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Peggy Levitt, The Transnational Villagers (2001), among migrants from Miraflores, Dominican Republic, and their community in Jamaica Plain, Boston); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to belonging. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: "Mobile people have weaker identities than settled people." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Mobility often produces strong, if changing, identities – Malkki's camp refugees, Basseri pastoralists, transnational villagers.
items.markingKey: Mobility often produces strong, if changing, identities – Malkki's camp refugees, Basseri pastoralists, transnational villagers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which a comparison of Malkki and Barth shows movement and belonging.
items.answer: Hutu refugees in Tanzania were forced to move and then confined in camps, while Basseri herders moved by choice along recognised routes. Both link identity to movement and space, but forced displacement produced a narrative of exile, while pastoral migration produced belonging through the route itself.
items.markingKey: Context (Hutu refugees in Tanzania were forced to move and then confined in camps, while Basseri herders moved by choice along recognised routes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Malkki's Purity and Exile and Barth's Nomads of South Persia, compare and contrast the role of power in movement and identity compared across ethnographies.
items.answer: Malkki's Purity and Exile (among Hutu refugees from Burundi who fled the 1972 killings, in Mishamo refugee camp and Kigoma township, Tanzania (fieldwork 1985–1986)): Camp administration regulated movement and livelihoods, and refugees' narratives of persecution were also a response to their marginal position. Barth's Nomads of South Persia (among Basseri pastoralists of Fars province, Iran (fieldwork 1958)): The chief (khan) coordinated the migration and mediated between the tribe, the state and settled villagers. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: "Movement is more important than place in shaping identity in the twenty-first century." Discuss with reference to at least one ethnography you have studied.
items.answer: Movement and place shape identity together; mobility often intensifies attachment to place.

items.stem: Explain why comparisons of movement should consider the role of the state.
items.answer: States determine who can move legally, settle, work or claim rights, so differences between ethnographies often reflect different relationships to state power.

items.stem: Explain why comparing elite and poor migrants is analytically useful.
items.answer: It shows that mobility is structured by class, citizenship and ethnicity: the same globalised world offers flexible citizenship to some (Ong) and deadly borders to others (De León, Holmes).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows that mobility is structured by class, citizenship and ethnicity: the same globalised world offers flexible citizenship to some (Ong) and deadly borders to others (De León, Holmes). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between compelled immobility and voluntary mobility.
items.answer: Voluntary mobility is chosen movement by those with the resources to move; compelled immobility is being forced to stay in place, as with refugees in camps or migrants without papers who cannot visit home.
items.markingKey: Voluntary mobility is chosen movement by those with the resources to move; compelled immobility is being forced to stay in place, as with refugees in camps or migrants without papers who cannot visit home. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the airport in Manila, two queues stand side by side at the departure hall. In one, Overseas Filipino Workers clutch brown envelopes of contracts and certificates, checked by an officer from the overseas employment agency. In the other, a family with Canadian passports moves straight to check-in. Marlon, a seafarer, tells me he has crossed twenty-six borders but has never been allowed off the ship in eleven of those ports. "I have seen the world," he says, "from the deck."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an international airport in the Philippines.

Compare and contrast how power is experienced by the people in the text and by the people in one other ethnography you have studied (for example Seth M. Holmes, Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies: Migrant Farmworkers in the United States (2013)). Keep the comparison running throughout rather than treating each case separately.
items.answer: Text: Mobility is structured by citizenship and class: passport holders move freely, while migrant workers are documented, checked and channelled by state agencies; Marlon's experience shows that crossing many borders can coexist with immobility (confined to the ship) – comparable to the contrast between Ong's flexible citizens and Holmes's farmworkers. Ethnography – Seth M. Holmes, Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies: Migrant Farmworkers in the United States (2013), with Triqui Indigenous migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and in California (fieldwork 2003–2005): Holmes uses Bourdieu's idea of symbolic violence to show how this hierarchy is naturalised: supervisors, doctors and sometimes workers themselves explain Triqui suffering by their bodies or culture rather than by labour conditions. Comparison: similarities and differences in how power is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The concept or question, such as "how movement shapes belonging", used to compare two ethnographies"?
options: camp-city
ethnic enclave
mobility regime
comparative frame
items.answer: comparative frame
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of comparative frame.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "humanitarian government"?
options: An urban neighbourhood where migrants of the same origin concentrate, with their own businesses and institutions
The process, often encouraged by states, of nomadic people settling permanently in one place
Michel Agier's term for the management of displaced populations by agencies combining care with control
The balance between forces that compel or block movement and people's capacity to choose how and where to move
items.answer: Michel Agier's term for the management of displaced populations by agencies combining care with control
items.markingKey: C. "humanitarian government" is Michel Agier's term for the management of displaced populations by agencies combining care with control.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "nomadism"?
options: Regular movement of people and their herds between pastures, usually along known routes and seasonal cycles
Michel Agier's term for the management of displaced populations by agencies combining care with control
The "tribal road" of the Basseri: their recognised migration route and the schedule for using it, described by Barth
The set of laws, technologies and practices that allow some people to move freely while restricting others
items.answer: Regular movement of people and their herds between pastures, usually along known routes and seasonal cycles
items.markingKey: A. "nomadism" is regular movement of people and their herds between pastures, usually along known routes and seasonal cycles.

items.stem: Leila writes: "Mobile people have weaker identities than settled people." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Mobility often produces strong, if changing, identities – Malkki's camp refugees, Basseri pastoralists, transnational villagers.

items.stem: Briefly explain why camp space shapes refugee identity.
items.answer: Bounded, administered camps separate refugees from local society, categorise them as a population and encourage shared narratives of exile (Malkki), while restrictions on movement and work create dependence.

items.stem: "Pastoralism is disappearing because it is inefficient." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Pastoralism remains productive in drylands; it is threatened mainly by land loss, borders, state policy and climate change rather than inefficiency.
items.markingKey: Pastoralism remains productive in drylands; it is threatened mainly by land loss, borders, state policy and climate change rather than inefficiency. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Movement always increases people's freedom." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Movement can be forced, dangerous and exploitative (De León, Holmes), and it can produce immobility, such as being trapped without papers.

items.stem: Distinguish between humanitarian care and humanitarian control.
items.answer: Humanitarian care provides food, shelter and health; humanitarian control registers, counts and restricts movement. Agier argues the two are combined.

items.stem: Explain the difference between transhumance and nomadism.
items.answer: Nomadism involves moving the whole community and herds across a range, often without fixed settlement; transhumance moves herds seasonally between fixed pastures, usually with a permanent home base.

Using the key concept of power, explain how the text illustrates unequal mobility. Make clear which key concept you are using and why it is relevant.
items.answer: Mobility is structured by citizenship and class: passport holders move freely, while migrant workers are documented, checked and channelled by state agencies; Marlon's experience shows that crossing many borders can coexist with immobility (confined to the ship) – comparable to the contrast between Ong's flexible citizens and Holmes's farmworkers.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Hodgson's Maasai in northern Tanzania shows change in pastoral societies.
items.answer: Development projects registered cattle to men and promoted ranching schemes, while land was lost to farms and conservation areas. State and development interventions transformed pastoral livelihoods and reduced women's rights over livestock.

items.stem: With reference to Aihwa Ong, Flexible Citizenship: The Cultural Logics of Transnationality (1999), explain how the key concept of identity helps us to understand movement and identity compared across ethnographies.

items.stem: Explain how Malkki's Purity and Exile illustrates the concept of identity. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: Camp refugees constructed a "mythico-history" in which they were the true, pure Hutu nation in exile, while town refugees adopted fluid, cosmopolitan identities and avoided the refugee label.

In the camp market, Abdi runs a shop made of corrugated iron that sells phone cards, pasta and solar lamps. He arrived as a boy in 1992 and his children were born here. items.stem:
Read the text below.

In late spring the Kyzyl family loads the yurt onto a Kamaz truck and drives the sheep up to the summer pastures, a journey that took two weeks on horseback in Grandfather Bolat's time and now takes two days. Bolat still rides behind the flock. His grandson films the move on his phone and posts it with the caption "nomad life". The pasture they use was assigned to a collective farm in Soviet times; now it is leased from the district office, and this year a mining company has fenced part of it.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a herding family in Kazakhstan.

Compare and contrast how change is experienced by the people in the text and by the people in one other ethnography you have studied (for example Piers Vitebsky, The Reindeer People: Living with Animals and Spirits in Siberia (2005)). Consider how the methods or theory of the ethnography might explain the differences.
items.answer: Text: Seasonal transhumance continues (summer pastures, flock movement, grandfather on horseback), but technology (truck, phone), Soviet collectivisation and post-Soviet leasing, and mining fences change how movement is organised and who controls land; the grandson's post shows identity as "nomad" being performed and valued even as practices change. Ethnography – Piers Vitebsky, The Reindeer People: Living with Animals and Spirits in Siberia (2005), among Eveny reindeer herders of Sebyan-Küöl, Sakha Republic (Yakutia), Siberia (fieldwork from 1988): Soviet collectivisation turned herding into state-farm work and sent children to boarding schools, and the collapse of the USSR in 1991 brought economic crisis to the herders. Comparison: similarities and differences in how change is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Ethnographies of movement show that structure matters more than agency."
items.answer: Structure sets the conditions of movement, but people exercise agency within them; the balance differs by case.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: borders, laws and markets compel or block movement (De León, Andersson). Arguments against: migrants choose routes, networks and identities (Levitt, Malkki's town refugees); pastoralists adapt mobility creatively (Chatty). Supported judgement: Structure sets the conditions of movement, but people exercise agency within them; the balance differs by case. Markbands (10 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem: "Power is central to understanding refugee camps and urban migrant communities." Compare and contrast two anthropological studies, for example Malkki's Purity and Exile and Agier's Managing the Undesirables, in the light of this claim.
items.answer: Malkki's Purity and Exile (among Hutu refugees from Burundi who fled the 1972 killings, in Mishamo refugee camp and Kigoma township, Tanzania (fieldwork 1985–1986)): Camp administration regulated movement and livelihoods, and refugees' narratives of persecution were also a response to their marginal position. Agier's Managing the Undesirables (based on fieldwork in refugee camps in Africa, including Kenya, Guinea, Sierra Leone and Zambia): "Humanitarian government" manages refugees as populations to be fed and counted, combining care with control. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: A student claims: "Mobile people have weaker identities than settled people." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Mobility often produces strong, if changing, identities – Malkki's camp refugees, Basseri pastoralists, transnational villagers.
items.markingKey: Mobility often produces strong, if changing, identities – Malkki's camp refugees, Basseri pastoralists, transnational villagers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that urban migrants have more agency than camp refugees. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: Both exercise agency within different constraints; the city offers more freedom but less protection.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: cities offer work, mobility and anonymity (Malkki's town refugees); urban migrants build networks and businesses; urban migrants face exploitation, racism and lack of protection (Bourgois); camp refugees also organise and resist. Suitable ethnographies include Malkki's Purity and Exile, Agier's Managing the Undesirables, Bourgois's In Search of Respect. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Both exercise agency within different constraints; the city offers more freedom but less protection. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Nomadic pastoralism has no future in the modern world."
items.answer: Pastoralism is under pressure but is adapting; its future depends on land rights and state policy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: land loss, borders and climate change threaten herding; young people move to towns; states promote settlement. Arguments against: pastoralists adapt using trucks, phones and markets (Chatty); pastoralism is efficient in drylands; Indigenous rights movements defend mobility. Supported judgement: Pastoralism is under pressure but is adapting; its future depends on land rights and state policy. Markbands (10 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem: "Can an anthropologist ever fully understand another way of life?" With reference to Malkki's Purity and Exile and the key concept of identity, evaluate possible answers to this question.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies identity explicitly and uses ethnography: Camp refugees constructed a "mythico-history" in which they were the true, pure Hutu nation in exile, while town refugees adopted fluid, cosmopolitan identities and avoided the refugee label. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.
